title: Three Boxes and Some Arrows
author: Jo Lein
summary: Jo Lein, a coach who wrote a book of behaviour frameworks and then returned to work in a middle school, reflects on how real schools test her own tidy models. The framework 'Identify, Disrupt, Replace' tells adults to get curious about what lies beneath a behaviour, but she admits that curiosity is much easier when you are not carrying a radio at 1:42 on a Tuesday. Distance from schools made patterns easier to see because she could not see every exception, whereas now the exceptions have names. She tells of a boy who keeps leaving class and who answers her question by saying he does better in the restrictive TRAICE setting, because there are fewer kids and less going on. His answer made her first interpretation look incomplete. The framework gave no solution, but it delayed her ready-made answer long enough to hear his. Her conclusion is that expertise can recognise a pattern, but it cannot finish the sentence for the person.
points: Frameworks that look elegant on a page are tested by the pressure of an actual school day, with bells, radios and several urgent problems at once.
Expertise makes you fast, but the speed can lead you to finish other people's sentences before they have told you what is going on.
A student who walks the halls told Lein he does better in the restrictive TRAICE setting, because there are fewer kids and less going on, which reframed his behaviour without excusing it.
The value of a framework may be less in solving the problem than in delaying the answer you already have long enough to hear the real one.
Distance gave her clear patterns, but closeness shows exceptions with names, and both views are needed.
quotes: Meanwhile, it’s 1:42 on a Tuesday. A kid won’t go to class. Another kid is crying for a reason you can’t tell is a serious safety concern or middle school nonsense. Someone needs me on the radio.
But there is something I did not fully appreciate when I was teaching other people to get curious about behavior: Curiosity is considerably easier when you aren’t also carrying a radio.
Eventually, you hear the first three sentences and start writing the fourth. You see the behavior and think you know the reason.
TRAICE is our more restrictive setting. It’s supposed to be a consequence—not the place a kid identifies as the environment where he is most successful.
This is exactly the kind of distinction I have spent years telling other people to make. Don’t stop at the behavior. Figure out what the behavior is doing for the person.
I know his answer made my original interpretation—kid who won’t stay in class—look embarrassingly incomplete.
But there is a difference between recognizing a pattern and deciding you already know the ending.
